# Exercise 6

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Exercise 6

In your new Quarto document, load `tidyverse` and `gt` libraries and read in `sleep_breakfast.csv` file using the pipe operator under the `data` folder. Inspect the data. What are the variables in the data? 
:::

```{r}
library(tidyverse)  # for data wrangling
library(gt)         # for pretty tables
read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv') %>% gt()
```

There are 4 variables in the data.

* SleepDuration	
* BreakfastPerWeek
* Class
* Campus

:::{.callout-caution}
## Common Mistakes: Incorrect Path

The following code will not run because R cannot locate where to read `sleep_breakfast.csv` from.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
read_csv('sleep_breakfast.csv')
```
:::

:::{.callout-caution}
## Common Mistakes: String Not Quoted

The following code will not run because the file name is not quoted as a string. The text should be enclosed in quotes to be recognized as a string. Note that string will be shown in green in default R syntax highlighting.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
read_csv(sleep_breakfast.csv)
```
:::

:::{.callout-caution}
## Common Mistakes: Ending the Pipe Incorrectly

The pipe operator needs a destination to send the output to. It cannot be left hanging without a function to receive the output.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv') %>%
```
:::

:::{.callout-caution}
## Common Mistakes: Double Use of `%>%` with a Temporary Object

This is not going to run because you are essentially trying to input the output of `read_csv()` twice into `gt()`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
df <- read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv')
read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv') %>% 
      gt(df)
```
:::


:::{.callout-caution}
## Common Mistakes: Pipe Operator in a New Line

Pipe operator should not start a new line by itself. It must be at the end of the previous line.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv')
%>% gt()
```
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Pipe Operator Alternatives

The following code chunks demonstrate different ways to pass the output of the `read_csv` function to the `gt` function. All of them achieve the same result.

**Option 1:** Use a temporary object `df` to store the output of the `read_csv` function. The con of this approach is that you will need to create and manage an additional object in your environment. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
df <- read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv')
gt(df)
```

**Option 2:** Instead of using a pipe operator, you can directly pass the output of the `read_csv` function to the `gt` function.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
gt(read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv'))
```

**Option 3:** Use the pipe operator to pass the output of the `read_csv` function directly to the `gt` function. `gt()` receives the output of the previous expression as its input (first input argument).

```{r, eval=FALSE}
read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv') %>% gt()
```

**Option 4:** You can also use the pipe operator with line breaks for better readability.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
read_csv('data/sleep_breakfast.csv') %>% 
      gt()
```

:::
